WILLFUL MISCLASSIFICATION OF INDEPENDENT CONTRACTORS — PENALTIES INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Lee · Acme Innovations LLC

INFORMATION AND BACKGROUND — WILLFUL MISCLASSIFICATION PENALTIES (LABOR CODE § 226.8)
This information sheet describes California's civil penalty scheme for "willful misclassification" of an employee as an independent contractor under Labor Code § 226.8. It is prepared in connection with a working relationship between Jordan Lee and Acme Innovations LLC.

Labor Code § 226.8 is a separate, narrower statute from the general test for whether a worker is an employee or an independent contractor in the first place (addressed in this corpus's own Independent Contractor Agreement document). Section 226.8 does not decide whether Jordan Lee is or was an employee or an independent contractor of Acme Innovations LLC. It instead describes what additional civil penalties, notice-posting duties, and other consequences California law attaches when a person or employer is separately found — by the Labor and Workforce Development Agency or a court — to have engaged in a specific, elevated form of misclassification that the statute calls "willful."

This information sheet does not itself determine that Acme Innovations LLC did or did not willfully misclassify Jordan Lee, does not investigate or make any finding about any specific working relationship, does not file anything with any agency or court, and does not initiate or constitute any legal proceeding.

THE STATUTE'S DEFINITION OF "WILLFUL MISCLASSIFICATION" AND THE CONDUCT IT PROHIBITS
California law makes it unlawful for any person or employer to willfully misclassify an individual as an independent contractor. It separately makes it unlawful to charge a fee, or make any deduction from compensation, against an individual who has been willfully misclassified — for example for goods, materials, space rental, services, government licenses, repairs, equipment maintenance, or fines arising from that individual's employment — where the charge or deduction would have violated the law had the individual not been misclassified.

The statute defines "willful misclassification" itself in specific, elevated terms: it means avoiding employee status for an individual by voluntarily and knowingly misclassifying that individual as an independent contractor. By this statutory definition, the penalties described elsewhere in this information sheet attach to a voluntary and knowing act of misclassification, as the statute itself defines that term — not, by this definition alone, to every instance of misclassification.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "(a) It is unlawful for any person or employer to engage in any of the following activities:(1) Willful misclassification of an individual as an independent contractor.(2) Charging an individual who has been willfully misclassified as an independent contractor a fee, or making any deductions from compensation, for any purpose, including for goods, materials, space rental, services, government licenses, repairs, equipment maintenance, or fines arising from the individual’s employment where any of the acts described in this paragraph would have violated the law if the individual had not been misclassified."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 226.8(a) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=226.8.)
  "“Willful misclassification” means avoiding employee status for an individual by voluntarily and knowingly misclassifying that individual as an independent contractor."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 226.8(i)(4) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=226.8.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of what conduct it prohibits and how it defines "willful misclassification" — not a claim about which state's law governs any specific working relationship, and not a claim that any specific person or employer did or did not willfully misclassify any specific individual within the meaning of this statute. Both citations below are to the same statutory section, Labor Code § 226.8, subdivisions (a) and (i)(4); that is disclosed here rather than presented as independent corroborating sources. This document does not independently verify, through reported case law, how courts have applied the "voluntarily and knowingly" standard to specific facts, or how it differs in practice from an employer's good-faith but mistaken classification decision; that question was not researched for this document. This document is informational only: it does not determine that any specific individual was willfully misclassified and does not determine the outcome of any specific matter.

CIVIL PENALTY RANGES: PER-VIOLATION AND ENHANCED PATTERN-OR-PRACTICE PENALTIES
If the Labor and Workforce Development Agency or a court issues a determination that a person or employer has engaged in willful misclassification or the related fee-charging conduct described elsewhere in this statute, California law sets a civil penalty of not less than $5,000 and not more than $15,000 for each violation, in addition to any other penalties or fines otherwise permitted by law.

The statute sets a separate, higher penalty range where the same kind of determination also finds that the person or employer has engaged in, or is engaging in, a pattern or practice of these violations: in that circumstance, the civil penalty is not less than $10,000 and not more than $25,000 for each violation, again in addition to any other penalties or fines otherwise permitted by law.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "(b) If the Labor and Workforce Development Agency or a court issues a determination that a person or employer has engaged in any of the enumerated violations of subdivision (a), the person or employer shall be subject to a civil penalty of not less than five thousand dollars ($5,000) and not more than fifteen thousand dollars ($15,000) for each violation, in addition to any other penalties or fines permitted by law."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 226.8(b) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=226.8.)
  "(c) If the Labor and Workforce Development Agency or a court issues a determination that a person or employer has engaged in any of the enumerated violations of subdivision (a) and the person or employer has engaged in or is engaging in a pattern or practice of these violations, the person or employer shall be subject to a civil penalty of not less than ten thousand dollars ($10,000) and not more than twenty-five thousand dollars ($25,000) for each violation, in addition to any other penalties or fines permitted by law."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 226.8(c) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=226.8.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the two civil penalty ranges it authorizes — not a claim about which state's law governs any specific working relationship, and not a claim about what penalty amount, if any, would apply to any specific violation. Both citations below are to the same statutory section, Labor Code § 226.8, subdivisions (b) and (c); that is disclosed here rather than presented as independent corroborating sources. This document does not address how many separate "violations" a given course of conduct is treated as constituting for penalty-stacking purposes, or what showing establishes a "pattern or practice" as opposed to a single violation; those questions were not researched for this document. This document is informational only: it does not determine that any penalty applies to any specific person or employer and does not calculate any specific penalty amount.

REFERRAL TO THE CONTRACTORS STATE LICENSE BOARD FOR A LICENSED CONTRACTOR
California law imposes an additional consequence where the person or employer found to have violated this statute is itself a licensed contractor under the Contractors State License Law. In that circumstance, the Labor and Workforce Development Agency or court, in addition to any other remedy already ordered, must transmit a certified copy of the order to the Contractors State License Board.

Once the registrar of the Contractors State License Board receives a certified copy of an agency or court order that resulted in disbarment under this referral requirement, California law requires the registrar to initiate disciplinary action against the licensee within 30 days of receiving it.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "(d) (1) If the Labor and Workforce Development Agency or a court issues a determination that a person or employer that is a licensed contractor pursuant to the Contractors State License Law has violated subdivision (a), the agency, in addition to any other remedy that has been ordered, shall transmit a certified copy of the order to the Contractors State License Board."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 226.8(d)(1) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=226.8.)
  "(2) The registrar of the Contractors State License Board shall initiate disciplinary action against a licensee within 30 days of receiving a certified copy of an agency or court order that resulted in disbarment pursuant to paragraph (1)."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 226.8(d)(2) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=226.8.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the referral and disciplinary-action requirements it imposes when a violator is a licensed contractor — not a claim about which state's law governs any specific working relationship, and not a claim that any specific person or employer is a licensed contractor or that any referral has occurred. Both citations below are to the same statutory section, Labor Code § 226.8, subdivisions (d)(1) and (d)(2); that is disclosed here rather than presented as independent corroborating sources. The statute's own text uses the word "disbarment" to describe the underlying order that triggers the registrar's 30-day disciplinary-action duty, without itself defining that term or cross-referencing the specific Contractors State License Law provision that authorizes disbarment as a licensing sanction; this document quotes that statutory language rather than independently verifying, through the separate Contractors State License Law provisions, the exact licensing consequence "disbarment" refers to there. This document is informational only: it does not determine that any specific contractor's license would be referred or disciplined and does not determine the outcome of any specific matter.

THE PUBLIC NOTICE-POSTING REQUIREMENT UPON A FINDING OF VIOLATION
When the Labor and Workforce Development Agency or a court issues a determination that a person or employer has violated this statute, California law requires — in addition to any other remedy already ordered — that the person or employer display a notice prominently on its internet website, in an area accessible to all employees and the general public; or, if it has no internet website, display the notice prominently in an area accessible to all employees and the general public at each location where a violation occurred.

The statute specifies what the notice must say: that the Labor and Workforce Development Agency or a court, as applicable, found that the person or employer committed a serious violation of the law by engaging in the willful misclassification of employees; that the person or employer has changed its business practices to avoid further violations; that any employee who believes they are being misclassified as an independent contractor may contact the Labor and Workforce Development Agency, with the agency's mailing address, email address, and telephone number included; and that the notice is being posted pursuant to a state order.

California law adds two further requirements for preparing the notice: an officer must sign it, and it must be posted for one year commencing with the date of the final decision and order.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "shall order the person or employer to display prominently on its internet website, in an area which is accessible to all employees and the general public, or, if the person or employer does not have an internet website, to display prominently in an area that is accessible to all employees and the general public at each location where a violation of subdivision (a) occurred, a notice that sets forth all of the following:"
  — Cal. Labor Code § 226.8(e) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=226.8.)
  "(1) That the Labor and Workforce Development Agency or a court, as applicable, has found that the person or employer has committed a serious violation of the law by engaging in the willful misclassification of employees.(2) That the person or employer has changed its business practices in order to avoid committing further violations of this section.(3) That any employee who believes that they are being misclassified as an independent contractor may contact the Labor and Workforce Development Agency. The notice shall include the mailing address, email address, and telephone number of the agency.(4) That the notice is being posted pursuant to a state order."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 226.8(e)(1)-(4) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=226.8.)
  "(f) In addition to including the information specified in subdivision (e), a person or employer also shall satisfy the following requirements in preparing the notice:(1) An officer shall sign the notice.(2) It shall post the notice for one year commencing with the date of the final decision and order."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 226.8(f) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=226.8.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the notice-posting requirement and its required content — not a claim about which state's law governs any specific working relationship, and not a claim that any specific notice has been or must be posted by any specific person or employer. All three citations below are to the same statutory section, Labor Code § 226.8, subdivisions (e), (e)(1)-(4), and (f); that is disclosed here rather than presented as independent corroborating sources. This document does not address enforcement of the posting requirement itself — for example, what consequence follows if a person or employer fails to post or maintain the required notice for the full one-year period — because the statutory text reviewed for this document does not itself specify a separate penalty for noncompliance with the posting requirement apart from the underlying violation. This document is informational only: it does not determine that any specific notice obligation currently applies to any specific person or employer and does not determine the outcome of any specific matter.

LIABILITY FOR A PAID ADVISOR WHO KNOWINGLY ADVISES MISCLASSIFICATION — AND ITS EXEMPTIONS (LABOR CODE § 2753)
California's willful-misclassification penalty scheme is not the only statute addressing who can be held responsible when a worker is wrongly classified as an independent contractor. A separate statute, Labor Code § 2753, addresses a paid advisor: it provides that a person who, for money or other valuable consideration, knowingly advises an employer to treat an individual as an independent contractor to avoid employee status for that individual is jointly and severally liable with the employer if the individual is later found not to be an independent contractor.

That advisor-liability statute states two exemptions from its own reach. It does not apply to a person who provides advice to their own employer. And it does not apply to an attorney authorized to practice law in California or another United States jurisdiction who provides legal advice in the course of the practice of law.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "(a) A person who, for money or other valuable consideration, knowingly advises an employer to treat an individual as an independent contractor to avoid employee status for that individual shall be jointly and severally liable with the employer if the individual is found not to be an independent contractor."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 2753(a) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=2753.)
  "(b) This section does not apply to the following persons:(1) A person who provides advice to his or her employer.(2) An attorney authorized to practice law in California or another United States jurisdiction who provides legal advice in the course of the practice of law."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 2753(b) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=2753.)
  Known gap: Labor Code § 2753 is a distinct statutory section from Labor Code § 226.8, which is the primary basis for the rest of this information sheet; it was fetched and verified separately, and this document draws it in because it is a closely related, distinctively named form of misclassification-related liability, not because it is part of § 226.8 itself. A researcher approaching this topic without checking the statutory text directly might reasonably assume that any "advising liability" provision would appear within § 226.8 — it does not; § 226.8's own text, as fetched and quoted elsewhere in this document, contains no reference to advisors, consultants, or anyone other than "any person or employer" who commits the underlying violation. Both § 2753 citations below are to the same statutory section, subdivisions (a) and (b); that is disclosed here rather than presented as independent corroborating sources. This document does not address case law interpreting "knowingly advises," what counts as "money or other valuable consideration," or how courts have applied the two exemptions to specific facts; that research was not conducted for this document. This document is informational only: it does not determine that any specific person or firm advised any specific employer regarding the classification of any specific individual, and does not determine the outcome of any specific matter.

WHO ENFORCES THIS STATUTE, HOW A PROCEEDING IS INITIATED, AND THE ELECTION-OF-REMEDIES RULE
California law authorizes the Labor Commissioner to enforce this statute and to issue a determination that a person or employer has violated it, following the same procedures set out in Labor Code Sections 98, 98.1, 98.2, 98.3, 98.7, 98.74, or 1197.1 — the general wage-claim and citation procedures administered by the Labor Commissioner's office. Enforcement under this statute may include investigating an alleged violation, ordering appropriate temporary relief to mitigate the violation or maintain the status quo while an investigation or hearing is pending, issuing a citation against a violating employer, and filing a civil action; where a citation issues, the procedures for issuing, contesting, and enforcing it follow the same rules that apply to citations issued under Section 98.74 or 1197.1. A public prosecutor, as the statute defines that term by reference to Labor Code § 181(a), may also separately enforce this statute by seeking the damages described below.

The statute also gives an enforcing party — the Labor Commissioner or a public prosecutor — the alternative of recovering, for each employee, the civil penalties described elsewhere in this statute as damages payable directly to the employee rather than as a civil penalty. But an employee is entitled to either recover those damages under this statute or to enforce a civil penalty under the separate Private Attorneys General Act provision, Labor Code § 2699(a), for the same violation — not both.

A "determination" under this statute, for all of the purposes described above, means an order, decision, award, or citation issued by an agency or a court of competent jurisdiction for which the time to appeal has expired and for which no appeal is pending.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "(g) (1) In accordance with the procedures set forth in Sections 98, 98.1, 98.2, 98.3, 98.7, 98.74, or 1197.1, the Labor Commissioner may enforce this section and issue a determination that a person or employer has violated subdivision (a). This enforcement of this section may include investigating an alleged violation of subdivision (a), ordering appropriate temporary relief to mitigate the violation or to maintain the status quo pending the completion of an investigation or hearing, issuance of a citation against an employer who violates subdivision (a), and filing a civil action. If a citation is issued, the procedures for issuing, contesting, and enforcing judgments for citations and civil penalties issued by the Labor Commissioner shall be the same as those set out in Section 98.74 or 1197.1, as appropriate. A public prosecutor, as defined in subdivision (a) of Section 181, may also enforce this section by seeking the damages described in paragraph (2)."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 226.8(g)(1) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=226.8.)
  "(2) In any enforcement pursuant to this subdivision, for each employee subject to Sections 98 to 98.2, inclusive, the Labor Commissioner under Section 98.3, 98.7, 98.74, or 1197.1, or a public prosecutor, as defined in subdivision (a) of Section 181, may alternatively recover the penalties set forth in subdivisions (b) and (c) as damages payable to the employee. An employee is entitled to either recover the damages as provided for in this section or to enforce a civil penalty, as set forth in subdivision (a) of Section 2699, but not both, for the same violation."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 226.8(g)(2) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=226.8.)
  "“Determination” means an order, decision, award, or citation issued by an agency or a court of competent jurisdiction for which the time to appeal has expired and for which no appeal is pending."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 226.8(i)(1) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=226.8.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of who may enforce it and how a proceeding under it may be initiated — not a claim about which state's law governs any specific working relationship, and not a claim that any specific enforcement proceeding has been or will be initiated regarding any specific person or employer. All three citations below are to the same statutory section, Labor Code § 226.8, subdivisions (g)(1), (g)(2), and (i)(1); that is disclosed here rather than presented as independent corroborating sources. This document does not independently verify, by fetching Labor Code §§ 98, 98.1, 98.2, 98.3, 98.7, 98.74, 1197.1, 181, or 2699 directly, the full content of those cross-referenced procedures and definitions; it reports only what § 226.8's own text says about them, which is the verified source for this clause. This document is informational only: it does not initiate any enforcement proceeding, does not determine that any specific person or employer has violated this statute, and does not determine the outcome of any specific matter.

California's willful-misclassification penalty scheme is not the only statute addressing who can be held responsible when a worker is wrongly classified as an independent contractor. A separate statute, Labor Code § 2753, addresses a paid advisor: it provides that a person who, for money or other valuable consideration, knowingly advises an employer to treat an individual as an independent contractor to avoid employee status for that individual is jointly and severally liable with the employer if the individual is later found not to be an independent contractor.

That advisor-liability statute states two exemptions from its own reach. It does not apply to a person who provides advice to their own employer. And it does not apply to an attorney authorized to practice law in California or another United States jurisdiction who provides legal advice in the course of the practice of law.

citations.quote: (a) A person who, for money or other valuable consideration, knowingly advises an employer to treat an individual as an independent contractor to avoid employee status for that individual shall be jointly and severally liable with the employer if the individual is found not to be an independent contractor.

citations.quote: (b) This section does not apply to the following persons:(1) A person who provides advice to his or her employer.(2) An attorney authorized to practice law in California or another United States jurisdiction who provides legal advice in the course of the practice of law.

California law authorizes the Labor Commissioner to enforce this statute and to issue a determination that a person or employer has violated it, following the same procedures set out in Labor Code Sections 98, 98.1, 98.2, 98.3, 98.7, 98.74, or 1197.1 — the general wage-claim and citation procedures administered by the Labor Commissioner's office. Enforcement under this statute may include investigating an alleged violation, ordering appropriate temporary relief to mitigate the violation or maintain the status quo while an investigation or hearing is pending, issuing a citation against a violating employer, and filing a civil action; where a citation issues, the procedures for issuing, contesting, and enforcing it follow the same rules that apply to citations issued under Section 98.74 or 1197.1. A public prosecutor, as the statute defines that term by reference to Labor Code § 181(a), may also separately enforce this statute by seeking the damages described below.

The statute also gives an enforcing party — the Labor Commissioner or a public prosecutor — the alternative of recovering, for each employee, the civil penalties described elsewhere in this statute as damages payable directly to the employee rather than as a civil penalty. But an employee is entitled to either recover those damages under this statute or to enforce a civil penalty under the separate Private Attorneys General Act provision, Labor Code § 2699(a), for the same violation — not both.

A "determination" under this statute, for all of the purposes described above, means an order, decision, award, or citation issued by an agency or a court of competent jurisdiction for which the time to appeal has expired and for which no appeal is pending.
